Sooner. In the late 1970s, Jean Riboud, the CEO of Schlumberger, was pondering in his Park Avenue office full of Rothko paintings: "can I create something BIG by putting Oil Services and chips together?" Having just acquired US chip company Fairchild for $425m, Riboud explicitly mentioned Artificial Intelligence in the company's 1979 annual report. All the stars seemed aligned, and a vision was set (even if the Fairchild acquisition proved a poor investment). Ahead of its 17 June Digital Day, SLB remains the most AI-advanced company in the industry.

Later. Our December 2025 view was that the Oil Services industry was about to catch up. Back in December 2025, we assessed the digital maturity of the O&G and Oil services industries with our colleague Richard Nguyen. We concluded that: 1) these two industries were VERY late in their adoption of AI/digital tools; and 2) that a catch-up did seem to be imminent (2026-27?).

Later. Our new May 2026 view – AI/Digital adoption may be delayed for longer (catch up in 2028-29?). Priorities have changed with the conflict in the Middle East. While the adoption of AI/Digital across the industry continues – and is even (slowly) accelerating – AI/Digital is no longer the major theme we had expected it to be in January 2026. Since March/April 2026, the CEOs of large oil services companies have been engaging extensively with governments, whose priorities have shifted dramatically towards security/diversity of supply and incremental energy infrastructures.

Human league. An O&G reservoir is a complex and evolving ecosystem that, like the human body, requires regular monitoring through repeated imaging (= seismic) and blood tests (= drilling). This is where AI can mainly bring additional revenue: more (quality) data → more hydrocarbons → increasing recovery rates.

The AI opportunity can be estimated at c.$5.6bn p.a. 1) It comprises both AI-related additional revenue (c.$1.0bn/18%) and cost improvements (c.$4.6bn/82%). 2) It can be split between Oil Field Services (OFS, c.$3.3bn/59%) and Engineering & Construction (E&C, c.$2.3bn/41%) companies. 3) The c.$3.3bn OFS opportunity may come from both cost improvements (c.$2.3bn) and revenue (c.$1.0bn). 4) The c.$2.3bn E&C opportunity is likely to come almost exclusively from cost improvements (c.$2.3bn), with little/no (c.$0bn) additional revenue.

Amara's law is unlikely to apply to Oil Services. Amara's law is the tendency to both; 1) overestimate the ST impact of a technology; and 2) underestimate its LT effects. In this report, we conclude that: 1) the O&G and Oil Services industries is very late with its Digital/Al adoption; 2) catch-up may now be delayed to 2028-2029, rather than 2026-2027; 3) the AI/Digital opportunity could nonetheless triple of the over the next 5 years, and may potentially add an incremental c.1.7% to EBITDA margins; 4) most of the gains may come from cost optimisations (rather than additional revenue); 5) regarding additional revenue, OFS in general, and seismic companies in particular, are better positioned; and 6) SLB (with a potential AI-related incremental boost to EBITDA/EBITDA margin of +8.7%/+1.9%), Viridien (+4.5%/+1.5%) and Technip Energies (+13.5%/+1.4%) are best positioned.

paragraph_content.content: The best definition of AI comes from our colleague Bob Brackett. He defines Artificial Intelligence as “electricity contemplating itself”. There are two advantages with this definition. First, it reflects the increasingly egoistic nature of AI – and particularly of Agentic AI (=AI systems capable of autonomous decision-making). Second, it looks at AI through the angle of growing associated energy demand. While electricity demand from Data Centers/AI was c.1,000 terawatt-hours in 2024 (=annual consumption of Japan), it is set to double to c.2,000 terawatt-hours by 2030 (=annual consumption of India).

AI training and energy demand are walking hand in hand. Quoting Bob: “training a single LLM next year is forecast to use the same energy as raising more than one million children to adulthood! - and by the way, estimates of training costs typically ring-fence the GPU and thus don’t include a comparable amount of energy to keep the data center cool, lit, and well operating”. Note however that the education/training of large LLMs are still at an early stage. In a recent essay (“Le temps de l’obsolescence humaine”), Bruno Patino, the CEO of Arte – a Franco-German cultural TV channel – states that “the largest LLMs can still be compared to four-year old children”.

paragraph_content.content: While most analysts focus on the demand side, we have always preferred to focus on the supply side. We believe that supply-side analysis is simply superior as demand can be volatile and unpredictable. Supply, on the other hand, offers the superior advantage of being fixed – at least in the short term! When you know that something is sure – even if it does not last – you should capitalize on it... Correct?

One of the most revealing overviews we have found on AI and the supply of Oil Services is provided by Aramco's CFO Ziad Al-Murshed in a September 2025 speech. We view this speech as truly insightful. "Applying AI has the potential to massively increase the capability to find more O&G, reduce development costs, and increase recovery rates". He highlighted that the highest value would be found in "operations" and within operations "in the reservoir". There may, however, be a bottleneck: "generating this value would be data intensive and requires massive computing power".

The impact of AI on the Oil Services industry is therefore about to evolve. Up to now, AI was essentially – and still remains today – an optimizer of internal costs, rather than a source of revenue. Globally speaking, we estimate the current AI opportunity for the entire Oil Services industry at c.$5.6bn, which can be split between cost optimization (c.$4.6bn) and additional revenue (c.$1.0bn) or between Oil Field Services (OFS, c.$3.3bn) and Engineering & Construction (E&C, c.$2.3bn) companies.

While this market may be tripling over the next five years to c.$17bn (OFS c.$10bn; E&C c.$7bn), AI is also likely to further widen the differences between OFS, where AI will be both an optimizer of costs and a source revenue, and E&Cs, where AI will mainly remain an optimizer of internal costs.

title_content.content: Dawn of the Al Oil & Gas Era

paragraph_content.content: In this future, the day in the field starts before sunrise, but the first ones to "wake up" are the Als. They scan live data from satellites, seismic sensors, wells and markets, and quietly adjust plans for drilling, production and maintenance. Engineers still come to work, but instead of sorting through reports, they walk into calm control rooms where large clear screens show only what truly matters, with the AI explaining in plain language what has changed and why.

Out at sea and in the desert, rigs and pipelines are watched over by swarms of small, tireless helpers. Drones fly inspection routes on their own, robots move along platforms and lines, and digital twins simulate every operation before it happens. When a pump starts to age or a valve shows a tiny leak, the AI spots it early, schedules a repair, orders the spare parts, and sends a technician with step-by-step guidance, turning what used to be emergencies into simple planned tasks.

From the wellhead to the refinery and finally to the customer, the whole value chain behaves like one coordinated system instead of separate islands. The AI balances production with demand, chooses cleaner operating modes, reduces emissions, and reroutes flows when a storm, a conflict or a price shock hits. People still make the big choices and set the rules, but the AI handles the complexity in the background, so the industry can be safer, leaner and more responsible while still delivering the energy the world needs.

title_content.content: VISION - HOW TOP EXECUTIVES SEE AI AND ITS IMPLICATIONS

paragraph_content.content: "Artificial Intelligence is as important for our future as the surge in oil exploration, it will change the order of magnitude in the size of our business" – Jean Riboud, Former CEO Schlumberger – 1979.
"AI is taking us into a new world of opportunities in terms of energy production and supply" – Ziad T. Al-Murshed, Executive Vice President & Chief Financial Officer – September 2025
"AI is electricity contemplating itself. Training a single LLM next year may use the same energy as raising more than one million children to adulthood!" Bob Brackett - October 2025.

Let's spend more time on Ziad Al-Murshed's visionary speech on “Reimagining Global Energy in a Digital Financial Future”. As it is SO INSIGHTFUL, we wanted to highlight some of the most important messages below. Note that this speech was made BEFORE THE WAR IN THE MIDDLE EAST.
"The world of energy is moving forward at speeds none of us has seen before – accelerated by a digital revolution, and led by breakthroughs in artificial intelligence".
"On one hand, the digital revolution is bringing substantial growth in energy demand. AI and digital centers will be responsible for about

of total world electricity demand growth between now and 2030. Demand from Data Centers and AI in 2024 was around 1,000 terawatt-hours, which is about the total electricity demand of Japan today. Demand in 2030 is expected to be over 2,000 terawatt-hours, which is about the total power demand of India today".
"On the other hand, this same revolution that will substantially contribute to the growth in demand, is also going to enable the energy sector to avail of more energy supply".
The largest value is in operations and, within operations, in the sub-surface (i.e. in the reservoir)
"In the oil and gas sector, the largest value potential is actually in operations, and within operations, the largest value potential is in the sub-surface — in the oil and gas reservoirs".
AI = Massive increase in capability...but is data-intensive and requires massive computing power.

"Applying AI in this field can massively increase the capability to find more oil and gas, and reduce development costs, and to increase recovery rates so that more of the found oil and gas is produced".

"THIS is where the AI revolution is enabling the energy industry to increase supply to help meet the energy demand that the AI revolution itself is increasing substantially! But generating this value is data intensive, and requires massive computing power".
Massive investments in sub-surface data acquisition and super computing power...

"In the energy industry, especially in oil and gas, this requires massive investments in sub-surface data acquisition and super computing power. It also requires investments in the oil and gas wells to install technologies that enable the actual optimization".
...so only a few players...and sole access is hugely important!
"These investments are so large, that relatively few industry players can justify making them — mainly players that have sole access to oil and gas reserves in order to be able to optimize them".

“Without sole access, optimization of a reservoir is not possible because neighboring producers would be drawing from the same reservoirs at maximum rates. Which is why the required massive investments in technology is not justified for any single producer among a group of producers that are accessing the same reservoir”.

“So with Big Data, digital infrastructure and talent, AI is taking us into a new world of opportunities in terms of energy production and supply. And they increasingly help us to deliver every bit of energy with the lowest possible cost, while continuing to lower emissions”
After Poetry and Vision, let's now turn to Applications.

AI has already started to have a meaningful impact on reducing costs in 1) exploration and development (seismic, subsurface data processing, reservoir simulation), and 2) in the automating of production processes (automatic, remote drilling operations). It also helps lower emissions.

title_content.content: THE O&G INDUSTRY - IT, OT, AI, CLOUD, EDGE COMPUTING

paragraph_content.content: In a joint report published in December 2025 with our colleague Richard Nguyen, we took a deep dive into the (very) late adoption of IT by O&G companies and concluded that:

item_content.content: - Annual IT spending by the O&G industry is (very) small compared to other industries: $45bn, i.e. only 1% of the world's total IT spending. By comparison, Banking/Investment Services is c.18%, Communication/Media is also c.18%, Manufacturing/Natural Resources is c.14%.

- While O&G E&P spending (c.$570bn) and O&G refining spending (c.$600bn) are somewhat similar, E&P IT spending ($19bn) is lower than Refining IT spending ($25bn). IT spending in the smaller (c.$50bn) midstream segment is limited to $1.5bn p.a.

- IT spending is expected to grow at 7.4% CAGR up to 2029 (\$60bn), with software spending (2025: \$12bn) being the fastest growing segment. This is still below the 8.4% CAGR expected for all the other industries combined (according to Gartner).

- AI adoption is still in its early stages. Only 13% of O&G groups have already deployed Agentic AI, and 49% plan to do so in 2026. The O&G industry faces many challenges (e.g., security, governance, IP protection, etc.) in the deployment/scaling of mission-critical systems, especially in Operational Technology (OT, hardware and software that control/monitor physical operations).

- The slow rise of immersive technologies. Immersive technologies include Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, and Mixed Reality. They represent the core of digital twins. Only 28% of O&G companies have already deployed these immersive technologies and 30% plan to do it over the next three years. Interestingly, 42% of them are still unsure or have shown little interest in them! The name of the game here is to go beyond digital twins and to adopt simulation twins. Simulation twins leverage AI and GenAI and use real-time data to simulate future outcomes (based on the current state + chosen parameters).

- As for any industry, but even more so in O&G, the name of the game is to integrate IT and OT and make them work together in a unified system: predictive maintenance and remote asset management leverage this IT/OT convergence the most.
- 57% of the industry is already using cloud solutions, while it is now gradually turning to edge computing (23% adoption).
- GenAI has, so far, been a source of frustration across the industry (as a lot of in-house data is not AI-ready yet).
- Agentic AI seems more promising. Following Adnoc's 2024 internal development (ENERGYai), SLB launched its Agentic AI tool (Tela) in November 2025.

title_content.content: WHAT DOES O&G VIEW GENERATIVE AND AGENTIC AI?

paragraph_content.content: We understand from our discussions that:

item_content.content: - O&G companies generally avoid implementing Generative AI (GenAI) in operational workflows until they can clearly control the related risks (e.g. security, governance, compliance, etc.). They need to have greater confidence in accuracy and intellectual property (IP) protection before any deployment, especially with mission-critical solutions.

- In more generic software applications (e.g. ERP, CRM, HR, etc.), these companies struggle to generate meaningful value from GenAI. Most projects do not scale well yet, because most data is not yet AI-ready (i.e. quality, consistency, security, and governance). These projects also compete with other projects for budget and resources.

- O&G companies are increasingly interested in Agentic AI's potential. However, they currently have only limited Agentic AI development resources. Most of their data and AI functions are geared toward delivering machine-learning-based solutions, and increasingly GenAI solutions. However, these companies believe that AI agents, combined with machine learning (ML) and automation, will help increase the intelligence of oil and gas assets.

- AI agents are goal-driven software entities that are granted autonomous decision-making and action-taking rights. In contrast to GenAI, AI agents can decide and take action independently. The effectiveness and value of AI agents should increase exponentially if many agents work together to tackle highly complex tasks that require greater coordination and cooperation.

- O&G CIOs are facing a significant governance challenge due to the proliferation of AI and the continued integration between IT and OT. They need to have a centralized organization that adapts technology stacks, data strategies, and governance structures to manage all types of AI from multiple sources that spread across more enterprise systems.

paragraph_content.content: In our view, the only way to (convincingly) assess the impact on AI on the entire Oil Services industry is to use a sample. Coal and oil brought about the industrial revolution because they provided abundant and cheap physical power. Microprocessors and memory will bring about a new revolution because they will provide abundant and cheap intellectual power". Source: Schlumberger's annual report, 1979.

While Jean Riboud believed that all Sciences Po graduates did share something special, he also knew that most of them would never ever become ‘geeks’. This was exactly our own personal situation before starting to write this report. Aside from partnering with experts - as we do in this report with our colleague Richard Nguyen - we needed to build our own - possibly naive or simplistic - framework (or at least a helpful metaphor). Our vision of Digital is that it could be represented as a city, a new city that we needed to visit and discover. This city is not built out of concrete and steel, but out of data. A place where every street connects workflows, every building hosts applications, and every network cable carries information. This is SLB’s digital city. The idea of this city was born from necessity. For decades, the O&G industry operated as isolated towns and villages - exploration, drilling, and production. Each village managed its own data in closed systems. Organizational silos and poor connectivity made working together slow and inefficient. Data were everywhere, but insights were trapped as the industry needed to overcome three series of challenges: 1) data complexity, 2) organizational / stakeholder constraints and 3) infrastructure and geographical limitations.

title_content.content: THE SIX LAYERS OF SLB'S DIGITAL CITY

paragraph_content.content: Starting from the bottom (the operational layer) and working our way up to the sixth level (the cognitive level), SLB's digital city can be thought of as a sandwich with six layers, each with a distinct purpose and offering. Below we compare it to day-to-day life in a city.

First Layer - The operational layer (= every morning I wake up and perform my daily tasks). Every morning, I get up, decide what I need to do, and start completing my tasks. Each action creates a little bit of information about how I live. Over time, I hopefully learn new things, adjust my routines, and get better at what I do - just as every operation in the field generates new data and improves the models that guide decisions in the future.

Second Layer - The infrastructure layer (= the foundations of the city). In order to live my day in the city, I need solid ground to stand on, the infrastructure that holds the city together. In the digital city, this invisible foundation is the cloud. It is the digital ground on which everything rests – the storage, computing power, and resilience that allow the city to exist. And when work happens far outside the city, edge computing extends this foundation outwards, so even remote places can stand on the same solid ground. The infrastructure is provided via partnerships, for instance with AWS or Azure, which ensure data scalability and global access.

Third Layer - The platform layer (= the transport connections). Every day, I use roads, metro lines, and sidewalks that work seamlessly, sometimes without noticing. But without these connections, the city would collapse into isolated blocks. In SLB's digital city, these standardized, interoperable pathways are what allow data to move across the E&P value chain - from planning to operations. This is underpinned by SLB's Operations Data Foundations (in partnership with Cognite, OSDU and Lumi).

Fourth Layer - The application layer (= the shops, doctors, lawyers and plumbers of the city). When I need groceries, medical help, legal advice, or a plumber, I look for the essential services that make city life possible. In the digital city, this is DELFI. It provides cloud-based tools for the different needs of an O&G operator - modelling, planning and field operations – very much the digital equivalent of the city's professionals.

Fifth Layer - The innovation layer (= the Forum in Ancient Rome). The Forum was where people met, exchanged ideas, traded, debated, and created new solutions. Every day, new possibilities took shape there. In SLB's digital city, this role is played by DELFI's open environment and Innovation Factory. External developers, clients, and partners can build, test, and deploy new solutions through APIs and collaborative frameworks, encouraging innovation inside the city's walls. In working together to get the most from these possibilities, this transforms SLB's digital city from a place that offers not just the necessities of life, but a city of people who want to thrive together.

Sixth Layer - The cognitive layer (= Tony Stark's J.A.R.V.I.S). The cognitive layer could be thought as the equivalent of having Tony Stark's J.A.R.V.I.S. at your fingertips: a reliable, trusted companion that understands context, anticipates needs, and expands your capabilities. A strong ally with a team of experts always on duty: analysts who never tire, advisors who draw inspiration from the collective knowledge, and assistants who can instantly provide the best options and solutions for any situation. Whether a resident is planning a new route to work, a shop is forecasting demand, or the city's caretakers are examining where resources are needed most, the cognitive layer provides guidance rooted in experience and historical data. With this cognitive layer, SLB's digital city has become truly intelligent.

title_content.content: SLB'S COGNITIVE LAYER = TELA AGENTIC AI

paragraph_content.content: At first glance, Tela may look similar to any other AI system. It can generate text, interpret data, and support decisions. However, its core design is fundamentally different. Operating within SLB's cognitive layer, Tela can seamlessly access and interact with applications across the SLB digital ecosystem—connecting insights to actions and enabling every part of the city to operate at its highest potential.

Like a human personality, AI is governed by an internal architecture that ultimately determines how it behaves. As this structure has evolved, the governing principles underpinning AI have moved from a linear one-step loop to a continuous feedback loop. Tela, as an agentic AI, is the latest development.

item_content.content: - Generative AI: the simplest form. You provide an input, and it generates an output. It is powerful but linear - a one-step loop that begins and ends with the prompt.
- AI Agents: a step further. They are designed for specific tasks. They can plan and act, based on predefined rules and workflows, and observe the results before completing the tasks.

- Agentic AI: begins by observing the environment (the data/resources available), rather than waiting for a prompt. It plans its next move, generates the required analysis, executes it, and learns from the outcome. It may also use multiple sub-agents to complete different parts of the workflow. The loop never stops, and each iteration improves the next.

paragraph_content.content: In this way, Tela orchestrates data across Lumi and Delfi to automate workflows and recommend decisions. It represents the transition from a digital city to an intelligent city, where each dataset improves the next, and where the system learns, predicts, and optimizes in real time.

We see AI as a transformational tailwind for Viridien's geoscience workflows for two fundamental reasons.

It will enhance interpretation: AI strengthens interpretation by producing cleaner, more structured, and more accessible geoscience data, particularly unstructured data. This means geoscientists can access:

item_content.content: - More accurate entity extraction from text (formations, sequences, wells)
- Corrected and fully digitized tables from poor-quality scans
- Correctly classified geological figures with contextual understanding

paragraph_content.content: These improvements directly elevate the quality of interpretation, enabling more confident technical evaluations and reducing rework.

It will shift scientists from low-value operational tasks to high-value activities: Traditionally, geoscientists spend significant time on manual data extraction, quality control, and classification before meaningful interpretation can begin. AI transforms this workflow by automating these low-value, time-consuming tasks, such as text recognition, table reconstruction, figure classification, and information retrieval, to deliver cleaner data pipelines and allow more time for technical reasoning. By automating repetitive tasks, AI reduces the burden on geoscientists and domain experts, enabling them to focus on interpretation and higher-order problem-solving.

paragraph_content.content: Beyond the energy sector, multiple industries' HPC requirements are expected to record a c.18% CAGR in 2022-2027.

High performance computing (HPC) combines specialized hardware, such as CPUs, GPUs, storage, and high-speed networking, with software and algorithms that are designed to tackle highly complex, compute-intensive tasks. Any workflow that requires large-scale processing effectively becomes an HPC application. As companies adopt machine-learning and integrate AI into their processes, they use far larger volumes of structured and unstructured data. This increases the computational load, creating a reinforcing loop: more AI adoption unlocks more data, which in turn drives greater demand for HPC.

paragraph_content.content: From consumption-based to outcome-based pricing.

- Consumption-based pricing: under this pricing model, customers are charged based on the amount of computing consumed—CPU hours, GPU hours, storage, bandwidth. As a result, the responsibility for efficiency is on the customer.

- Outcome-based pricing: customers pay for a finished output. In this way, Viridien, the provider, takes responsibility for efficiency and performance, while the customer focuses on the business outcome, not for optimizing computing power. In other words, the customer pays for certainty and expertise, not computing consumption.

Traditional on-demand GPU per hour pricing is highly variable across providers (it is not within the expertise of the customers to optimize the computing power), making it difficult for customers to predict their potential costs. As data-intensive workflows continue to grow, we see Outcome-as-a-Service as directly addressing the cost uncertainty by linking pricing to the delivered result. In our view, this model matches Viridien's strengths in algorithmic expertise, optimized HPC environments, and deep domain knowledge with the customer's need for certainty, efficiency, and predictable costs, enabling the company to differentiate from "commodity" GPU pricing.
